Your agent ran all night and wrote 30,000 lines of code. Every check passed. The app was broken. The loop didn't fail — your system did, because nothing in it could stop and ask if you were still solving the right problem. You already did the smart thing and split one agent into a team: a planner, a builder, a reviewer. That's the graph. But connecting agents isn't the same as putting someone in charge. The fix isn't a smarter model — it's a governance layer, an operating system for your agents. And the part you can build today is simple: every decision in your system has exactly one owner.

→ Countable things belong to CODE — budget limits, retry counts, valid JSON, tests passing; never ask a model to check what an IF statement can
→ Ambiguous things belong to the MODEL — why did this fail, the plan or the reviewer; let it diagnose, never let it decide alone
→ The mission belongs to YOU — not an approve button, the one person who owns what "done" actually means
→ That overnight disaster didn't need more intelligence; it needed code to stop the bleeding, a model to say why, and a human holding the goal
→ You already built half an operating system by accident — checkpoints, retries, permissions; the other half you build on purpose
→ A graph connects your agents. An operating system runs them.

ZE1KEgsm_80.description:
Uber just shipped an AI agent that builds your whole grocery cart from a photo of a handwritten list — and the interesting part for builders is how little the LLM actually does.

Their real architecture is a multi-prompt state graph, and most of the boxes are plain deterministic code. The LLM only handles the fuzzy stuff: reading what you meant, judging which product fits. Everything that has to be correct — prices, arithmetic, availability, the cart total — is code the model never touches.

→ The planner LLM doesn't "go shopping" — it emits a structured CartPlan (item, search_terms, item_context, price constraints), then hands it to code
→ "12 eggs" resolves to one carton of twelve via a deterministic quantity step, not free LLM arithmetic
→ A deterministic guardrail can veto a bad output and fall back before it ever reaches your cart
→ The lesson: when an agent is unreliable, the fix usually isn't a bigger model — it's taking responsibility away from the model and moving anything exact into code

The rule to steal: LLM handles meaning, code handles truth.

jZMBjAtSKi0.description:
What would actually happen if the Sun were instantly replaced with a black hole of the exact same mass?

The instinctive answer is that Earth and every other planet would get pulled in and destroyed. That instinct is wrong, and it comes from a common misconception about how black holes work. Contrary to popular belief, black holes are not cosmic vacuum cleaners that suck in everything nearby. Outside of a certain distance, a black hole's gravity behaves identically to any other object of the same mass. Gravitational force depends on exactly two things, an object's mass and your distance from it, and in this scenario, neither has changed. The planets' masses stay the same, and the black hole has the same mass the Sun always had.

This means every planet in the solar system would continue on its current orbit, completely unaffected. Earth would keep circling once a year, exactly as it does now, just around a black hole instead of a star.

The only physical difference is size. The Sun currently has a radius of about 700,000 kilometres. A black hole of the same mass would collapse down to a radius of roughly 3 kilometres. One additional, subtle change would actually happen, Mercury's orbit currently wobbles very slightly due to the Sun's uneven internal density. A black hole is essentially a perfect point mass, so that wobble would stop entirely.

But losing the Sun as a light and heat source would still be catastrophic. Photosynthesis would stop almost immediately, and without any energy input, the entire solar system would begin cooling toward near absolute zero. Every living thing would eventually die, not from falling into the black hole, but from the cold.

A group of AI researchers just published a 90-page plan for what should happen if AI becomes smarter than every human on earth.
The team includes former OpenAI researchers. They did conversations with frontier AI lab employees, policymakers, national security experts, and wrote AI 2040: Plan A.
The proposal is simple to explain and incredibly difficult to pull off.
Get the US and China to agree to delay the development of superintelligence until 2040. Make almost all frontier AI research public. Let dozens of companies catch up instead of allowing a handful of labs to race ahead. And enforce all of it.
The timeline they have is wild.
By 2028, AI companies are pushing to automate fields like law the way they pushed into coding a few years earlier. By 2029, the US and China negotiate a deal. By 2030, AI research has become fully automated, but the agreement slows the race before an intelligence explosion happens.
It's one of the most interesting pieces of AI policy writing I've read this year.

-IrWlbs3FGI.description:
We didn't have footage, but the images of the crash on the Moon have finally arrived, the upper stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket that struck the lunar surface, exactly as predicted in our earlier update.

South Korea's Danuri orbiter, operated by the Korea Aerospace Research Institute, captured before-and-after images of the exact impact site, observing the location for about 30 minutes before the collision and another 30 minutes right after, eight observations total. The after-images clearly show a brand new crater that wasn't there before.

Independently, the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope in Chile detected two distinct elements in the impact plume, sodium and lithium, each reflecting sunlight differently enough to be told apart. The lithium came from the rocket itself. The sodium came from the Moon's own surface, blasted out on impact.

Two completely independent confirmations, images and chemistry, of the exact same event.

The stage hit at 8,700 kilometres per hour. NASA's latest estimate puts the new crater at roughly 18 metres wide and nearly 4 metres deep. For scale, a natural meteoroid carrying the same energy hits the Moon about once every six days, this wasn't a rare event, we simply knew exactly when and where this one was coming.

NASA and ESA are both still processing their own data, with more observations expected soon.

Source: Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI), Danuri Mission. European Southern Observatory, Very Large Telescope Observations. NASA, Falcon 9 Upper Stage Lunar Impact Analysis.

72zrUOzf1C8.description:
Our solar system briefly had ten planets, and almost nobody remembers the tenth one.

For a short window, the official list read Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto, and Eris. Eris is a trans-Neptunian object with an unusually eccentric orbit, ranging from about 37.9 AU at its closest to roughly 97.5 AU at its farthest from the sun, more than double Pluto's average distance. At its most distant point, temperatures drop low enough that Eris's thin atmosphere condenses and freezes onto its surface as a layer of snow, then thaws again as it swings back closer to the sun.

Before Eris was confirmed in 2005, astronomers had a working assumption, icy trans-Neptunian objects were reliably smaller than Pluto. Eris broke that assumption. It turned out to be roughly 27 percent more massive than Pluto, despite having a slightly smaller diameter, making it denser overall. It also has its own moon, Dysnomia, discovered later that same year.

Eris is named after the Greek goddess of strife and discord, a fitting choice, since its discovery caused exactly that within the astronomical community. The existence of an object rivaling Pluto in mass forced the International Astronomical Union to formally define what a planet actually is for the first time. Under the new 2006 definition, Pluto no longer qualified. Today, both Eris and Pluto are officially classified as dwarf planets.

Source: NASA, Eris Overview. International Astronomical Union, 2006 Planet Definition Resolution. California Institute of Technology, Discovery of Eris (Brown, Trujillo, Rabinowitz).

vFyvzJLcCR8.description:
Only one spacecraft has ever visited Pluto, and it didn't even land, it flew past.

It took NASA's New Horizons probe nine years to reach Pluto after launching in 2006, arriving in July 2015. Before that, the best imagery we had came from the Hubble Space Telescope, low-resolution and unable to resolve any real surface detail. New Horizons changed that entirely, revealing a surface far more geologically complex than anyone expected.

Among the discoveries: Sputnik Planitia, a heart-shaped nitrogen ice glacier roughly a million square miles wide and up to 2.5 miles thick, possible cryovolcanoes, water-ice mountain ranges, canyon systems hundreds of miles long and over two miles deep, and evidence pointing to a subsurface liquid water ocean beneath the icy crust.

Pluto's atmosphere is so thin it barely qualifies as one, and surface temperatures drop to around minus 229 degrees Celsius. Pluto has five known moons, the largest of which, Charon, is over 1,200 kilometres across, more than half Pluto's own diameter and larger than the dwarf planet Ceres. Charon is massive enough that it and Pluto don't orbit each other in the traditional sense, both bodies orbit a shared centre of gravity, or barycenter, that sits outside Pluto's surface. The two are also mutually tidally locked, permanently facing each other.

Pluto's orbit is tilted about 17 degrees relative to the plane the rest of the planets follow, and it's also highly eccentric, between 1979 and 1999, Pluto was actually closer to the Sun than Neptune was. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet, specifically because it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood, the combined mass of other Kuiper Belt objects sharing its zone outweighs Pluto by roughly 14 times.

Pluto was named in 1930 by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl from Oxford, England.

Source: NASA, New Horizons Mission Overview. NASA, Pluto Facts. International Astronomical Union, 2006 Resolution B5.
#Pluto #NewHorizons #DwarfPlanet #Charon #NASA

It's called Cuddle-Fish, from Keio University with the MIT Media Lab. Most robots unsettle us, stiff bodies and almost-human faces that land right in the uncanny valley. shadcn, the god of UI on the internet, just dropped new chat interface components. And before building them, he published 15 rules for what makes a great streaming chat experience.
Almost every single one is about scroll behavior.
Here are some of my favorite rules.
Never move the reader against their intent. If someone’s reading, don’t pull them somewhere else. Auto-scroll should never be the default.
If they’re at the live edge, keep the stream in view. If they scroll away, leave them there.
When images load, markdown expands, or code blocks render, none of that should make the reader lose their place.
He turned all of this into a single component called MessageScroller.
It handles anchored threads, streamed replies, restored conversations, prepended history, jump-to-message, scroll controls, and visibility tracking.
All the scroll behavior that almost every AI chat app gets wrong.
Install it with this one command and you're good to go.

BYEeWlHoExE.description:
Google's new robot unscrews a lightbulb nine times out of ten and loses to a trash bag more than half the time, and that one gap tells you which jobs get automated first.

Google DeepMind shipped Gemini Robotics 2 on July 30, and unlike most robot announcements it published the failure rates instead of only the highlight reel. Read those numbers side by side and a very clean line appears. It is not strength and it is not intelligence. The only thing that decides whether a task is basically solved or still years away is whether the object keeps its shape when you touch it, and whether it stays where you left it. Two yeses and the robot is already good at it. One no and it falls off a cliff.

→ Unscrew a lightbulb 92%, precise part insertion 89.6%, pick something off a shelf 76.3% — all rigid, all holding still
→ Tie a trash bag 44%, seal a ziplock 40%, sweep with a dustpan 32% — all soft, all changing shape as the hand closes
→ Same object, different place: off a shelf 76.3%, off the floor 45.7% — the floor hides where the thing actually is
→ Yes, the demo really did tie a knot in a bag, and DeepMind is the one who reported that it works 44 times out of 100
→ So sorting rigid parts, machine tending and packing kits are the jobs that go first
→ And laundry, food prep, bin bags and cable runs are the ones that are still years out

Comment "FLOPPY" and I'll send you the docs link.
Which job in your life is actually floppy?

Everyone talks about better prompts = better AI outputs.

But if you're building AI apps or using LLMs seriously, there's a much bigger question:

How do you know if the AI's answer is actually good?

In this video, we break down 6 essential LLM evaluation metrics:

1. Correctness — Is the answer actually accurate?

2. Groundedness — Is the AI using the information provided, or inventing facts?

3. Relevance — Did the AI actually answer the question?

4. Completeness — Did it cover every important part of the request?

5. Conciseness — Is the response clear and to the point, without unnecessary information?

6. Safety — Is the AI avoiding harmful or dangerous outputs?

These metrics become especially important when you're building AI applications, RAG systems, AI agents, chatbots, or production LLM workflows.

Because prompting an AI is only half the problem.

The other half is knowing whether the output deserves to be trusted.

Xnj5ta_JxLE.description:
Landing on Mars isn't science fiction anymore, it's something we've done repeatedly with robotic missions since 1976, though no human has made the trip yet.

Scientists believe Mars once closely resembled early Earth. Orbital and rover imagery has revealed ancient river channels, dried lakebeds, and geological evidence consistent with a past ocean covering parts of the northern hemisphere. Over billions of years, Mars lost most of its atmosphere and surface water, leaving behind the dry, iron-oxide-covered world we see today, the source of its distinctive red colour.

Mars is home to Olympus Mons, the largest known volcano in the solar system, standing approximately 21.9 kilometres tall, about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest, with a base roughly the size of Arizona. Nearby lies Valles Marineris, a canyon system stretching over 4,000 kilometres in length and reaching depths of up to 7 kilometres, more than ten times longer and several times deeper than Earth's Grand Canyon.

Average surface temperature sits around minus 63 degrees Celsius, dropping to as low as minus 140 at the poles during winter.

Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, both thought to be captured asteroids. Phobos is gradually spiraling inward due to tidal forces and is expected to either collide with Mars or break apart into a ring system within the next 30 to 50 million years.

One of the most actively studied Martian mysteries involves methane detected by NASA's Curiosity rover, which fluctuates seasonally in ways not yet fully explained. Researchers have not determined whether the source is geological activity or, potentially, biological processes, making it a key focus in the ongoing search for evidence of life.

A Martian day, called a sol, lasts approximately 24 hours and 37 minutes, remarkably close to an Earth day.

Source: NASA, Mars Facts and Exploration. NASA Curiosity Rover, Methane Detection Studies. Wikipedia, Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

eYrMF9Cht8A.description:
Today's AI models keep getting smarter, but every conversation still feels like their first day on the job. Trajectory co-founder Arjun Karanam calls this the experience gap: models are improving on IQ, but not on experience. Continual learning aims to close it, turning the trillions of tokens of agent interactions that get thrown away into signal that makes agents better with every use.

At Sequoia Capital’s Own Your Intelligence event, Arjun lays out four goals for companies that want to get there: full traceability (including sub-agents and corrective behavior like edits and retries), evals drawn from real production traffic, harnesses that let agents orchestrate rather than constrain them, and getting comfortable running on open weights. He also covers what should be trained into the model versus left to the harness, and how to learn from interactions without training on customer data.

AI in digital marketing helps teams predict behavior, personalize experiences, generate creative, automate media decisions, and estimate impact — but its effectiveness depends less on the model than on the quality of the data and the clarity of the objective. In this video, we walk through 12 real examples from brands like L'Oréal, Meta, Sephora, Amazon, HubSpot, Spotify, and Coca-Cola, and pull out the transferable lesson behind each one. 🤖

Not every automation is AI. A rule fires the same way every time; a model changes its output based on what the data says. We break down where that distinction actually matters — and how to measure incrementality instead of just AI activity.

✅ Key takeaways:
• An AI system trained on low-value conversions gets highly efficient at acquiring more low-value conversions
• AI-generated personas are hypotheses, not market research — validate before they shape positioning
• CTR is an intermediate measure; look at incremental purchases, margin, and retention
• AI output is production, not value — measure financial impact against a control group or baseline
• The durable advantage isn't access to a model; it's cleaner first-party data, faster testing, and governance that keeps customer trust
